books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Abraham Lincoln, speech to the Illinois Republican State Convention, Springfield, June 16, 1858

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, speech to the Illinois Republican State Convention, Springfield, June 16, 1858; public domain.
stimulus.text:
“We are now far into the fifth year, since a policy was initiated, with the avowed object, and confident promise, of putting an end to slavery agitation. Under the operation of that policy, that agitation has not only, not ceased, but has constantly augmented. In my opinion, it will not cease, until a crisis shall have been reached, and passed — “A house divided against itself cannot stand.” I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free. I do not expect the Union to be dissolved — I do not expect the house to fall — but I do expect it will cease to be divided. It will become all one thing, or all the other.”
— Abraham Lincoln, speech to the Illinois Republican State Convention, Springfield, June 16, 1858

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Abraham Lincoln, “House Divided” speech (1858), public domain
stem: What did Lincoln predict would happen to the United States?

options.text: The Union would break into two separate nations that would never rejoin or reconcile with each other.
options.misconception: Lincoln says he does not expect the Union to be dissolved; he expects it to stop being divided.

options.text: The Southern states would voluntarily give up slavery within a few years, without any war at all.
options.misconception: Lincoln predicts the nation will become all one thing or all the other, not that the South will give up slavery on its own.

options.text: The nation would stop being half slave and half free, becoming all one thing or all the other.
Slavery would fade away quietly because no one would argue about it anymore in the country.
options.misconception: Lincoln says the agitation has constantly grown, not faded.

rationales.A: Lincoln says he does not expect the Union to be dissolved or the house to fall.
rationales.B: Nothing in the passage promises that the South will give up slavery by choice.
rationales.C: Lincoln says the government “cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free,” and that it “will cease to be divided” by becoming “all one thing, or all the other.” Background: he spoke in 1858, three years before the Civil War settled the question by ending slavery.
rationales.D: Lincoln says the agitation has “constantly augmented,” the opposite of fading away.
rationales.general:
1. Read Lincoln’s sentence plainly. The government “cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free.”
2. Read what he expects instead. It will “cease to be divided” and become “all one thing, or all the other.”
3. Rule out a split. Lincoln says he does not expect the Union to be dissolved or the house to fall.
4. Name the prediction. The nation would end its division over slavery by becoming wholly free or wholly slave.
Remember: a prediction is a claim about the future, so test it against what actually happened next.
